svg.text: TRAFFIC CONTROL — THE SIGNAL STATE MACHINES
THE PHASE CYCLE — this is the machine that actually runs
the initial phase, set in the ctor
phase = (phase + 1) % 4 — one step per tick(), 1 second apart
THE INVARIANT, read straight off the table: in every one of the four rows, at most ONE axis is green. ✓
Lights are only ever assigned in axis PAIRS (setPair(signal, north, south)), so N and S can never disagree, and the two
axes are always assigned in the same statement. Conflicting greens are impossible by CONSTRUCTION, not by a runtime check.
What the table does NOT have: an all-red clearance between phase 1 and phase 2. Phase 1 yellow flips straight to phase 2
green on the crossing axis. Real junctions insert a 1-2s all-red so late traffic clears the box. Easy to add: make it 6 phases.
Also missing: pedestrian phases, protected left turns, and any per-approach timing. Every phase gets exactly one tick.
phase is a raw int with an if/else-if chain in applyPhase(). An enum carrying its own (nsSignal, ewSignal) pair would
make the table declarative and make "add a phase" a one-line change instead of another branch.
tick() and both emergency methods are synchronized on the Intersection — the phase field never tears.
THE SignalState CHAIN — built, but not plugged in
Intersection.applyPhase() calls light.setSignal(signal), which REPLACES the state field with a brand-new object.
It never calls light.advance(), the one method that walks next(). So RED → GREEN → YELLOW → RED is dead code today.
And durationMs() is read by nobody: the controller ticks every 1s no matter what any state says it wants.
To wire it up: give Intersection an elapsed-time budget per phase, compare it against the active state's durationMs(),
and call advance() when it expires. Then green can genuinely last 4s while yellow lasts 1s.
EMERGENCY — the override that outranks the cycle
tick() returns early — the phase FREEZES
green drops to red with no
exitEmergency RESETS to phase 0 rather than resuming where it froze — after any incident the N-S axis always goes first.
Defensible (a known state is better than a guessed one), but say it is a choice. A group fans emergency to every child at once.

g.text: THE TICK IS THE DESIGN DECISION WORTH DEFENDING
TrafficController exposes both start() — a ScheduledExecutorService firing every second — and tickOnce(),
the exact same step invoked by hand. Every test drives tickOnce() and never starts a thread: no sleeps,
no flakes, no waiting four seconds to watch one light turn.
That is the same trick as an injected clock: separate "what advances the system" from "who decides when".
Production gets the scheduler; tests get the loop. One code path, two drivers.
The gap to close: scheduleAtFixedRate is a FIXED 1s regardless of what any SignalState asks for. Until
durations are honoured, "green lasts 4 seconds" is a comment, not a behaviour — and a demo will show
green, yellow, red all lasting exactly one tick each.
